section_summary: This section documents Japanese military intelligence-gathering and propaganda activity in Germany during 1932–1933. It includes reports of disguised Japanese army officers inspecting German industrial machinery, two substantial pro-Japanese publications defending Japan’s position in Manchuria, and observations about Japanese diplomatic personnel in Berlin. The final documents concern anti-American comments attributed to Japanese Embassy staff and a Japanese Club bulletin defending Japan’s naval policy under the Washington and London treaties.

people.name: Leon Dominian
people.role: American Consul General in charge at Stuttgart

people.name: Wilhelm Solf
people.role: Former German Ambassador to Tokyo and pro-Japanese lecturer; rumored author of the Manchuria pamphlet

people.name: Max Schmit

people.role: Professor at the Imperial University in Kyoto and author of a French-language defense of Japan’s Manchurian policy

subfiles.title: Visit to Factories by Japanese
subfiles.from: Leon Dominian, American Consulate General, Stuttgart
subfiles.about: Reports suspected Japanese army officers inspecting specialized machinery at the Robert Bosch factory near Stuttgart.
subfiles.summary: Dominian reports Japanese visitors posing as merchants questioned Bosch factory officials, who suspected army officers; Bosch's Berlin branch said they worked for the Japanese Military Attaché's large staff.

subfiles.title: Shipments of War Materials to Japan: Cross-Reference to Despatch of March 3, 1932
subfiles.about: Cross-references a Stuttgart report concerning German shipments of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a March 3, 1932 despatch citing a March 2 communist newspaper article on war-material shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Shipments of War Materials to Japan: Cross-Reference to Despatch of March 4, 1932
subfiles.about: Cross-references a further press-based report about German shipments of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a March 4, 1932 despatch with press information on shipments of war materials from Germany to Japan.

subfiles.title: Japanese Propaganda
subfiles.from: Frederic M. Sackett, American Embassy, Berlin
subfiles.about: Transmits and evaluates two examples of Japanese propaganda circulating in Germany about Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Sackett forwards a pamphlet and sheet on Manchuria from the Japanischer Verein, distributed by the Japanese Embassy; the tactless propaganda drew criticism, and he calls Attaché Banzai exceptionally active and intriguing.

subfiles.title: Japan und die Mandschurei
subfiles.about: Summarizes Georges Bonneau’s arguments defending Japan’s intervention and position in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: German-language article justifying Japan's Manchuria position by wars and treaty rights, comparing U.S. interventions, listing alleged Chinese violations, and stressing Japanese investment.

subfiles.title: Betrachtungen zur Mandschurei-Frage
subfiles.about: Presents an extensive German-language defense of Japanese influence and military action in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The pamphlet argues that Japanese power brought order, economic development, infrastructure, and protection from civil war and Bolshevism to Manchuria, while China benefited from mass migration into the region. It portrays Japan’s military operations as defensive enforcement of treaty rights and criticizes China’s boycotts, competing railways, violence against Koreans, and inability to maintain order. Later sections defend Japan’s position under international law and before the League of Nations, endorse Manchurian self-government, and present extensive population, investment, railway, and trade statistics.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Despatch No. 1616 and Japanese Naval Propaganda
subfiles.about: Calls attention to Japanese Embassy hostility toward the United States and recommends reading a bulletin’s explanation of Japanese naval policy.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum on Despatch No. 1616: Japanese Embassy staff in Berlin made nearly hostile comments about the U.S.; Part II of the translation clearly, if speciously, states Japan's naval treaty position.

subfiles.title: Transmitting News Bulletin Issued by the Japanischer Verein in Deutschland
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, American Consulate General, Berlin
subfiles.about: Transmits Japanese Club bulletin No. 273 and reports increasingly hostile comments about the United States by Japanese diplomats in Berlin.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith reports Japanese Embassy staff in Berlin grew hostile toward the U.S., using the Japanischer Verein as a propaganda channel, and notes a commercial attaché's recall for his German parentage.

subfiles.title: Japanischer Verein in Deutschland Bulletin No. 273
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese diplomatic and policy news and defends Japan’s naval construction under the Washington and London agreements.
subfiles.summary: Bulletin No. 273 announces Ambassador Nagai's Hamburg visit and argues Washington and London naval ratios disadvantaged Japan, which stayed within treaty limits.

subfiles.title: English Translation of Japanischer Verein in Deutschland Bulletin No. 273
subfiles.to: American diplomatic and Department of State readers
subfiles.about: Provides an English translation of bulletin No. 273 on Japanese diplomacy, economic policy, and naval armaments.
subfiles.summary: The translation covers Ambassador Nagai’s Hamburg visit, consultations between War Minister Araki and Finance Minister Takahashi, Japanese demands for naval parity, and a proposed petroleum self-sufficiency program. The naval article traces the ratios established by the Washington Conference and London Agreement and argues that they required Japanese restraint and vessel destruction while allowing American expansion. It concludes that Japan’s naval construction remained within treaty limits and focused mainly on lighter vessels, submarines, transports, oil-supply ships, and naval aviation.
